identity.title: Resting heart rate >100/min (and postural pulse increment)

technique.how: Count the radial or apical pulse for 30-60 s after at least 2 minutes at rest (supine); tachycardia is >100/min. For the postural component, keep the patient supine 2 minutes, then standing 1 minute, and record the pulse rise; a rise of 30/min or more, or inability to stand because of dizziness, is positive.
technique.prerequisites: Patient rested; note beta-blockers, pacemaker, and pain/anxiety.
technique.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is hypotensive, has suspected hip/spine fracture, or is at high fall risk.

interpretation.positive_finding: A large postural pulse increment (>=30/min) or severe postural dizziness is highly specific for large-volume blood loss; resting tachycardia is present in about three-quarters of patients with cardiac tamponade but is nonspecific across shock, PE, sepsis, anemia, and thyrotoxicosis.
interpretation.negative_finding: Supine tachycardia is frequently absent after moderate blood loss, so a normal resting rate does not exclude hypovolemia; a normal postural pulse response has modest value after moderate blood loss (composite sensitivity 22%).
interpretation.pitfalls: Beta-blockers, pacing, athletic training, and autonomic neuropathy blunt tachycardia; fever, pain, anxiety, and drugs cause tachycardia without hypovolemia; the postural test is unsafe in unstable patients.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive postural increment: treat as significant hypovolemia/hemorrhage; resting tachycardia: prompts search for cause (PE, tamponade, sepsis, bleeding) rather than a specific diagnosis.

estimates.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade among patients with known pericardial effusion (tachycardia present)
estimates.population: Pooled studies of patients with known tamponade or referred for pericardiocentesis with known effusion (8 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Echocardiographic/hemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade (varied by study)

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min, for large blood loss (phlebotomy)
estimates.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled from 10 studies of postural vital signs; large blood loss category)
estimates.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy (large blood loss as defined by the review)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.97/(1-0.98) = 48.5; LR- = (1-0.97)/0.98 = 0.03; from the abstract's sensitivity 97% and specificity 98%; CIs not computed
estimates.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min, for moderate blood loss (phlebotomy)
estimates.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (moderate blood loss category)
estimates.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy (moderate blood loss as defined by the review)
estimates.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)

sources.citation: Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with a pericardial effusion have cardiac tamponade? JAMA. 2007;297(16):1810-8.
McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-9.
Chunilal SD, Eikelboom JW, Attia J, Miniati M, Panju AA, Simel DL, Ginsberg JS. Does this patient have pulmonary embolism? JAMA. 2003;290(21):2849-58.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform postural measurements in hypotensive, syncopal, or fall-prone patients; do not use resting heart rate alone to exclude hemorrhage in beta-blocked or elderly patients.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Tachycardia with hypotension, elevated JVP, or pulsus paradoxus suggests tamponade or massive PE; with fever suggests sepsis - escalate immediately.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Pulse counting is reproducible; no kappa extracted for postural increment.

extraction_notes: Resting tachycardia alone has no defensible sens/spec/LR in the visible abstracts: McGee 1999 states supine tachycardia is 'frequently absent' after up to 1150 mL blood loss but gives the 33% sensitivity figure only for supine hypotension, so no resting-tachycardia estimate for hypovolemia is entered. The postural entries are COMPOSITES (dizziness OR pulse increment >=30) from healthy-volunteer phlebotomy, not ED patients; the abstract gives one specificity (98%) that I attached only to the large-loss entry. Moderate/large blood-loss volume definitions are in the JAMA tables (not accessible); (unverified recall) approximately 450-630 mL vs 630-1150 mL. Roy 2007 tamponade sensitivity is from studies of patients with known tamponade/effusion (no specificity possible). Chunilal 2003 (PE RCE) abstract reports no tachycardia accuracy; PIOPED clinical findings paper (Stein 1991, PMID 1909617) abstract also lacks a heart-rate figure, so no PE estimate is entered.
